claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was a Christian monk and ascetic who lived from approximately 345 to 399 AD.
Evagrius was born in Ibora in Pontus and was ordained as a reader by Basil of Caesarea and later as a deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus.
Evagrius served as archdeacon in Constantinople and participated in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.
Evagrius left Constantinople for Jerusalem around 382, where he became a monk in the monastic communities of Rufinus and Melania the Elder, taking monastic vows in 383.
Evagrius spent the remaining years of his life in the Egyptian desert, in Nitria and Kellia, where he wrote extensively on asceticism.

De octo spiritibus malitiae (On the Eight Spirits of Wickedness) is a brief treatise of eight chapters, one for each evil thought: gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, and pride.
Each chapter of De octo spiritibus malitiae contains mostly brief aphorisms, frequently set in pairs, occasionally punctuated by longer discursive paragraphs.
Evagrius's advice in De octo spiritibus malitiae on how to combat the evil thoughts is filled with metaphorical imagery and intended to be read slowly and contemplated.
The work was transmitted under the name of Nilus of Ancyra in some manuscripts.
The Greek text of De octo spiritibus malitiae survives in the Patrologia Graeca.
Evagrius developed a meticulous taxonomy of evil thoughts, their origins, and the physical experiences associated with them, arranging his works in an ascetic curriculum for the training of monks.

Evagrius was one of the most influential theologians in the late fourth-century church and his development of a theology of contemplative prayer and asceticism laid the groundwork for a tradition of spiritual life in both Eastern and Western churches.
